accepted.question_text: For Type Ia supernovae—supernovae whose ejecta lack hydrogen and helium—what direct or circumstantial evidence can establish whether their progenitors are moderate-mass binary systems, given that the proposed white-dwarf progenitors and possible companions are too faint for routine pre-explosion or post-explosion identification?

evidence.quote: Common wisdom has it that SNIa originate from moderate mass binary systems (e.g. [8]), but what is the evidence for binarity?
- The absence of H and He from SNIa ejecta points in the direction of highly evolved progenitors.

The fact is that we have never seen any such star actually exploding, nor can we expect a detection any time soon because white dwarfs are faint stars and even their companions are not expected to be particularly bright stars.
We are left with circumstantial evidence, but we have to make it as solid as possible before concluding that "we know what the progenitors are"

accepted.question_text: Among possible Type Ia supernova progenitors with initial masses about 3–8 solar masses, which stellar properties—especially high rotational velocities and magnetic fields in B-type main-sequence stars—can determine whether a star ends by exploding as a Type Ia supernova, with or without a companion?
accepted.context_brief: Stellar properties controlling Type Ia explosions

evidence.quote: As mentioned before, it is most reasonable that SNIa progenitors are stars in the approximate range of 3-8 M⊙, i.e. stars that on the Main Sequence belong to spectral types B.
Many of these stars are known to display high rotational velocities, and may be expected to have high magnetic fields as a result of intense dynamo activity.
Perhaps some of these properties may be THE cause for a given B-type star to end its evolution exploding as a SNIa, whether with or without the help of a companion.

accepted.question_text: For stars of roughly 3–8 solar masses that become Cepheid variables after leaving the main sequence and later pass through a planetary-nebula phase, can systematic observations of white-dwarf companions to Cepheid variables determine the statistical properties and crucial parameters of binary systems that can produce Type Ia supernovae?
accepted.context_brief: Cepheid companion constraints on Type Ia progenitors

evidence.quote: Moreover, stars in the mass range 3-8 M⊙ are known to become Cepheid variables when they evolve off the main sequence and to end their regular evolution through a Planetary Nebula phase.
Perhaps there are important clues to the nature of SNIa progenitors that can be extracted from the study of stars easily identifiable in these characteristic phases.

For example, a systematic study of the white dwarf companions of Cepheid variables would permit us to clarify the statistical properties of binary systems that may give origin to a SNIa and help identifying the crucial parameters that lead to a SNIa explosion.

accepted.question_text: Why does the empirical Type Ia supernova standardization relation work—brighter Type Ia supernovae evolve photometrically more slowly than fainter ones—and how much cosmological bias can arise if the high-redshift population has a different balance of fast progenitors with lifetimes under about 100 million years and tardy progenitors that typically explode more than 1 billion years after formation?
accepted.context_brief: Physical basis and redshift evolution of Type Ia standardization

evidence.quote: Even if SNIa are commonly referred to as ideal standard candles because of their high luminosity at explosion and their relatively narrow range of observational properties, they are not quite perfect and, maybe, not even standard.
Standardization is obtained exploiting the empirical evidence that bright SNIa evolve photometrically more slowly than faint SNIa.

However, even if this phenomenon is measured rather accurately in the local Universe so as to lead to accurate empirical corrections, its physical nature is far from understood and, therefore, this standardization rests on unsecure grounds.

Moreover, when moving to higher redshifts [7] , i.e. to the past phases of the evolution of the Universe, the balance between fast evolving SNIa progenitors (with lifetimes less than about 100 Myrs) and the “tardy" ones (that typically explode more than 1 Gyr after formation) shifts in favor of the fast component, so that any systematic difference between the two components will bias the observational results.

accepted.question_text: What are the true progenitor types and stellar masses of Type Ib/c core-collapse supernovae, and how can they be identified despite their rarity, greater typical distances, Hubble Space Telescope resolution limits, and optical photometry that provides only weak lower limits on pre-explosion bolometric luminosity or stellar mass?

evidence.quote: Core-collapse supernovae (CC-SNe) are believed to originate from the collapse of the core of massive stars (M> 8M⊙) at the end of their nucleosynthetic life when Iron has formed in the core of the star and there is no additional energy source to prevent the star from collapsing onto itself catastrophically.

Trying to do the same for SNIb/c has not been as successful, mostly because these events are more rare and, therefore, are likely to be discovered in more distant galaxies so that even HST resolution is not enough to provide an unambiguous identification of the progenitor star.

However, just because of being high effective temperature stars, photometric measurements in few optical bands do not allow one to determine pre-explosion bolometric luminosities and/or stellar masses.

While these results seem to be consistent with theoretical and statistical expectations, one has to consider that a lower limit is hardly good enough to clarify the issues but can at best reduce the parameter space within which one has to look for THE correct answer.

accepted.question_text: For the core-collapse supernova subclasses SNIIb, SNIIn, and SNIIL, are their progenitor masses located in the apparent 16–20 solar-mass gap between measured Type IIP progenitors of about 8–16 solar masses and Type Ib/c lower limits above about 20 solar masses, or are those explosion types mainly determined by other parameters such as binarity or rotation?

evidence.quote: Type IIP SN progenitors, leading to the identification of red supergiant progenitors and to explicit mass determinations for about a dozen SNe, which fall in the range ∼ 8M⊙ to ∼ 16M⊙.
The few lower limits indicate that the targeted SNIb/c had progenitors with masses above ∼20 M⊙.
Still we don’t know much about the remaining multiplicity of CC-SNe, such as SNIIb, SIIn, SNIIL.

The progenitor mass estimates for SNIIP and SNIb/c leaves unanswered the question "are the progenitors masses of SNIIn, SNIIL, SNIIb falling in the apparent gap 16-20 M⊙ or are these SN explosions mostly determined by some other parameter, such as binarity, rotation, etc?"

accepted.question_text: For faint core-collapse supernovae, how faint can the faintest events be, where does the observational and physical boundary between nova and supernova phenomena fall, how numerous are faint supernovae, and how many unexpected supernova explosion channels exist?

evidence.quote: It is intuitive that if there is a category of faint CC-SNe, one may miss many, or most of them unless looking very hard.
The studies championed by Benetti, Pastorello, and their group have shown that some SNII can be really faint, as faint as MB ≃ −14 and perhaps even fainter [17].

Despite their valuable efforts and results (many of them presented at this Conference), we are seeking quantitative answers the the questions: “How faint can “faint" SNe be?", “Where is the boundary between Nova and Supernova phenomena fall?", “How many “faint" SNe are there?", and “How many “unexpected SN explosion channels exist?"

accepted.question_text: For ultra-bright Type II supernovae, how bright can the brightest events be, what physical class are they, and why do they occur; in particular, can pair-annihilation explosions of ultramassive stars above about 140 solar masses and extremely low metallicity below about one-thousandth solar metallicity explain such events in the local universe after more than 13 billion years of chemical evolution?

evidence.quote: At the other end of the scale, it is clear that exceptionally bright SNII do occur, starting with “my" first SN, 1979C, which at maximum was at least as bright as a SNIa (MB < −19.5) [1], to the very recent SN 2005ap [19] and 2006gy [20].
These events pose a number of question, such as “How bright can “ultra-bright" SNe be?", “What are they?", “Why do they occur?", etc.
One of the “simple" suggestions is that they are the result of a pair-annihilation event which is predicted for ultramassive stars (M> 140M⊙) of extremely low metallicities (Z< 1/1000Z⊙).

This is an interesting possibility that is worth considering and pursuing, but I find it hard to imagine that such stars may exist in the local Universe, after more than 13 billion years of chemical evolution.

accepted.question_text: What is the final fate of the most massive stars with initial masses approximately 30–40 to 100 solar masses: do they produce very faint explosive events, quietly disappear into black holes, and can such disappearances be detected by monitoring nearby galaxies for bright stars that vanish?
accepted.context_brief: End states of the most massive stars

evidence.quote: Another open problem is what happens to the most massive stars, i.e. those stars with initial masses in the approximate range 30-40-up to 100M⊙.
They are supposed to end their lives as black holes and, possibly, end in a quite unspectacular event.
So, one is presented with the questions: “Do these stars explode producing very faint events or do they just “disappear"?, and “Can we detect such events?".
Therefore, one should monitor at regular intervals a suitably large number of reasonably nearby galaxies and record which bright stars have disappeared.

accepted.question_text: What physical conditions determine the gamma-ray-burst/supernova connection: why do many supernovae, including Type Ic events, not produce observable gamma-ray bursts, and why do many gamma-ray bursts lack associated supernovae?

evidence.quote: It is now well established that a number of Gamma-Ray Burst (GRB) sources have associated SNIc counterparts (e.g. [24]) and that both SNIc and GRBs are most closely associated with active star forming regions than any other type of explosive sources [25].

However, only a handful of GRBs-SNIc associations have been recognized so far and, despite all efforts, there are GRBs that are positively not associated with any SN, e.g. GRB 060614 for which it has been excluded the association with any SN brighter than -13.7 [22, 23], and many SNIc that have not shown evidence of any conspicuous gamma-ray emission (e.g. [24]).
Therefore, we are presented with two complementary and fundamental questions: “Why many SNe are not GRBs?", and “Why many GRBs are not SNe?".
Only answering these questions, we could claim that we do understand the GRB-SN connection.

accepted.question_text: How should stellar-evolution models leading to supernova explosions incorporate rotation and magnetic fields for progenitors with original masses above 3 solar masses, including B-type and O-type stars?
accepted.context_brief: Rotation and magnetic fields in supernova models

evidence.quote: First, it seems to me that, since all SNe appear to originate from progenitors with original masses above 3 M⊙, i.e. B-type or O-type stars, both rotation and magnetic fields can be crucially important and should explicitely be folded in the theorical model evolution that leads to a SN explosion.

accepted.question_text: How does the supernova phenomenon evolve with metallicity, stellar population, cosmic age, environment, and other relevant parameters across cosmic time, and how should those dependencies be included when using supernovae to understand how the universe works and evolves?

evidence.quote: While studying any type of SN and any aspect of their explosions, one should also consider the cosmic evolution of the SN phenomenon as a function of important parameters such as (i) metallicity, (ii) stellar population, (iii) cosmic age, and (iv) environment.
The point is that we are not studying SNe just to understand SNe, but rather because we want to understand how the Universe works and evolve.

accepted.question_text: What physically grounded classification scheme for supernovae should replace or supplement purely morphological subclass definitions so that newly observed diversity does not create the false impression that distinct explosion problems have been solved merely by assigning new subclass names?

evidence.quote: Also, I recommend that the SN community should devise (and enforce...) a classification that is based on Physics rather than pure morphology.

Defining new subclasses and/or catchy names every time something different is found may not help much to the understanding of the complex phenomen of SN explosions, and may slow down the progress in some fields by creating the illusion that a problem has been solved.
